Contact (sparśa) refers to the six groups of contact.
Feeling refers to the six bodies of feeling.
Craving refers to the six bodies of craving.
Grasping refers to the four graspings.
"Existence" (bhava) refers to the karma that can give rise to existence in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
"Birth" (jāti) refers to the arising of the aggregates (skandhas) within existence.
"Old age" (jarā) refers to the maturation of the aggregates.
"Death" refers to the dispersal and disintegration of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Question:
For what reason are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance?
Why is there old age and death conditioned by birth? Answer:

Because ordinary persons here, in the absence of an interval [of awakening], do not know the Four Noble Truths, they long and night after night delight in and cling to the five aggregates of clinging as "I" and "mine. Thus, through that which has been contacted, they form the thought: "This is mine," "This is my self," and "This is my body. In this way, there is a joyful attachment to pleasure, and through their conjunction, there arises volitional formation (*saṃskāra*).
That which is conditioned by volitional formations (saṃskāra) is not the domain of wisdom; it comes into being through attainment and abides within existence, like a seed sown in a well-tilled field.
When that consciousness is absent, existence ceases.
This is called "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations.

Those volitional formations arising from that ignorance consist of intentions that enter into attachment to the signs of existence; they become an accumulation and give rise to continuity within the process of becoming.
Consciousness (vijñāna) follows the mind within existence and is not severed; therefore, volitional formations (saṃskāra) condition consciousness.

Just as there is no light without the sun, yet it grows while abiding upon the earth, so too, without consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) would have no basis for growth. They are like reeds leaning against one another, mutually dependent.
Therefore, consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Depending on this basis, the remaining names arise together, and the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) increases;
depending on name, life, the four great elements, and the condition of nutriment at the time of eating, the remaining five sense-bases arise and increase.
Since nothing else serves as this condition, it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.
Through the coming together of the remaining faculties, their objects, and consciousness, contact arises; therefore, "the six sense bases condition contact."
Through contact, one experiences either suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
It is not the case that what is contacted [itself] is the feeling; therefore, contact is the condition for feeling.
Deluded ordinary persons, having experienced pleasure, become attached to it and further seek out the experience of suffering, while seeking pleasure as its antidote.
If one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is equanimity; therefore, feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because one grasps at objects of craving with intense thirst, craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*).
Since that grasping acts as the seed for existence, grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*).
Because one is born into various realms of existence as determined by the predominance of karma, there is birth.
Because birth gives rise to old age and death, birth is the condition for old age and death.
Just as grain serves as the condition for seed, so too should it be understood that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Just as the seed is the condition for the sprout, so should consciousness be understood as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Just as the sprout is the condition for the leaf, so should name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) be understood as the condition for consciousness.
Just as the leaf is the condition for the branch, so should name-and-form be understood as the condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Just as a branch is the condition for a tree, so should it be understood that the six sense bases are the condition for contact.
Just as a tree is the condition for a flower, so should it be understood that contact is the condition for feeling.
Just as a flower is the condition for sap, so should it be understood that feeling is the condition for craving.
Just as gruel is the condition for rice, so should it be understood that craving is the condition for grasping.
Just as rice is the condition for the seed, so should it be understood that grasping is the condition for becoming.
Just as the seed is the condition for the sprout, so should it be understood that becoming is the condition for birth.
In this way, various continuities arise; thus, their prior limit is unknowable, and their subsequent limit is also unknowable.
In this way, ignorance arises as the primary causal condition for continuity; its prior limit is unknowable, and its subsequent limit is also unknowable.
Question:
What is the condition for ignorance? Answer:

Only ignorance serves as the condition for ignorance; latent dispositions serve as the conditions for outbursts, and outbursts serve as the conditions for latent dispositions; the former acts as the condition for the former, and the latter for the latter.
Furthermore, all afflictions collectively constitute the condition for ignorance.
As the Buddha has said:
"From the accumulation of outflows arises the accumulation of ignorance.
Furthermore, it is like the single dharma of the mind: when the eye sees a form, a deluded person gives rise to craving.
At this time, the delusion of the mind regarding what is pure and pleasant is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

This attachment through volition is "conditioned by ignorance, there are formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*). This attachment of the mind is "conditioned by these formations, there is consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*).
The mental factors associated with consciousness and the form derived from them constitute "name-and-form" conditioned by consciousness.
From feeling arises joy; because of this joy, and because of the conditions of joy and form, the sense faculties become purified—this is called "the six sense bases" conditioned by name-and-form.
Ignorance-contact is the condition for the six sense bases; conditioned by contact, there is pleasant contact, which conditions feeling.
Conditioned by feeling, there is craving, through which one clings to pure pleasure.
This craving conditions clinging, through which one clings to volitional formations. With that as a condition, becoming arises; with becoming as a condition, birth arises.
Abiding is already aging; the dissolution of mindfulness is death.
In this way, the twelve links of dependent origination are established within a single moment.
Question:
Among those twelve links of dependent origination, how many are designated as afflictions?
How many are designated as karma? And how many are designated as karmic fruition?
How many are past?
How many are future?
How many are present?
How many conditions?
How many have already arisen?
What are the conditions?
What is the dharma of causes and conditions?
What is the distinction between these two?
And what is the nature of defilement through causes and conditions?
Answer: Three afflictions—ignorance, craving, and grasping;
two karmas—formative action and existence.
The remaining seven are the fruits of retribution.
In this context, that which is called "affliction" acts as the cause for the existence of future birth, just like the colors of a painter.
These phenomena do not arise of themselves, just like the work produced by the painter's colors.
The afflictions cause [the process] to arise; with conditions present, birth occurs, just as there are various forms.
Two factors belong to the past: ignorance and volitional formations.
Two factors belong to the future: birth and old age and death.
The remaining eight [factors] exist in the present.
In this way, by taking these three time periods, the continuity of birth and death from beginningless time can be understood.
One should not speak of "twelvefold dependent origination," nor should one speak of anything other than the twelvefold dependent origination.
What, then, is the conditionality (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
Because these twelve factors serve as causes for one another in successive order, this is called conditionality.
It gives rise to the twelve links of dependent origination; it is the dharma that has arisen.

Regarding the distinction between these two: as for "causes and conditions," it refers to the differentiation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); it is not established and cannot be described, nor should it be said to be either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because they give rise to the practice of dependent origination, the conditioned has already been established; this is the distinction between these two dharmas.
As for the cause and condition of the nature of defilement: by means of this practice and by means of this characteristic, ignorance and formations are established.
Conditioned by those formations, those signs, and that nature, those noble ones do not rely on anything else, but penetrate them with clear wisdom.
All such things as these are called the defiled nature of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, this causal condition can be understood through seven aspects:
namely, by way of three sections, four summaries, twenty lines, the wheel, the drawing forth, the analysis, and the inclusion of characteristics.
What are the three sections?
Formations and consciousness constitute the first section;
sensation and craving constitute the second section between them.
Existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*) constitute the third link.
Regarding the past, karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as conditions for the present fruit of retribution; this is the first link.
Using the present fruit of retribution as a condition for present afflictions is the second link.
Taking present afflictions as conditions for future retribution constitutes the third section.

The first and third sections—those concerning cause and effect and those concerning existence—are "with-existence" (sabhava) sections; the second section—concerning effect and cause—is a "non-existence" (asabhava) section.
What is the meaning of "having intervals"? Answer:

It refers to those who, until their final passing, have not yet transcended the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), due to the conditions of afflictions from their initial karma.
There is further birth within the various realms of existence; this is called the "link of birth.
Question:
How is it established?
Answer: That person enters into association with ignorance and craving while performing meritorious deeds.
For such an ordinary person of evil karma, this is what is called "death" at that time.

Suffering through death, one lies placed in the place of the dead; seeing neither this world nor the world beyond, losing mindfulness and failing to regain it—at that time, one undergoes the suffering of birth.
The wisdom of mental intention declines, and physical vigor declines; the faculties gradually fail.
From the body, whether from above or below, the life-faculty fails and withers away, like the drying of a tala leaf.

At this time, as in a dream, one engages in karma through four factors: the action (*karma*), the characteristics of the action (*karmalakṣaṇa*), the destination (*gati*), and the characteristics of the destination (*gatilakṣaṇa*).
What is karma? It is that which is performed—whether meritorious or non-meritorious, heavy or light, much or little.
Just as when one approaches that which was first created, that karma arises.
Regarding the characteristics of karma: in whatever place the karma is performed based upon, in that very place its companions arise.
When the characteristic of karma arises, it may at times manifest as the performance of an action.
As for the destination (*gati*), a happy rebirth (*sugati*) arises through meritorious conditions, while an unhappy rebirth (*durgati*) arises through non-meritorious conditions.

Regarding the characteristics of the destination (*gati-nimitta*): at the time of entering the womb, birth occurs through the conjunction of three factors; for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), birth occurs in dependence on a particular place. That which arises as the place of birth may be a palace, a seat, a mountain, a tree, or a river; it arises according to the specific destination and in accordance with the shared grasping of its characteristics.
At that time, having gone there, whether leaning, sitting, or lying down, he sees it or takes it.

At that time, the initial karma and its characteristics, as well as the destination and the characteristics of the destination and their activities, arise and cease with a rapid mind; at the moment of death, departing swiftly, immediately after that rapid mind, together with the cessation of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the end is accomplished.

At the end, through the sequence of the mind without interval, it arises swiftly; it performs its function by means of that very karma, or the sign of that karma, or the sign of a realm of existence (*gati*), or the sign of grasping (*upādāna*).
The resultant mind then passes into a subsequent existence, like one lamp lighting another, or like fire emerging from a fire-gem.
Because those joints arise from the mind, they are like companions.
Within the mother’s womb, based upon the impurities of the father and mother, thirty material forms produced by karma arise; these reside within the body in ten locations.
In that state, during the moment of aging (*jarā-kṣaṇa*), there is no mind; forty-six material phenomena (*rūpa*) arise.

These consist of thirty produced by karma (*karmaja*), two produced by nutriment (*āhāraja*), and eight produced by the moment of non-mind (*acittaka*). At the moment of aging, together with the second moment of mind, fifty-four material phenomena arise.

Thirty moments [of consciousness] are produced by karma; three moments and eight [moments] are produced by nutriment. Thus they arise: consciousness conditions name-and-form, and name-and-form conditions consciousness.
In this way, existence is established with joints; herein, it should be understood that three joints are formed.
Question:
How is it summarized by means of the four? Answer:

Ignorance and formations are a summary of past karma and afflictions; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are a summary of present fruition; craving, grasping, and becoming are a summary of present karma and afflictions; and birth and old age and death are a summary of future fruition.
Thus it may be understood through these four summaries.
Question:
How [is it understood] by means of twenty aspects?
Answer:
By grasping at past ignorance and craving, one forms the grasped object through the characteristic of affliction;
by grasping at past formations and becoming, one forms the grasped object through the characteristic of karma.
By taking up consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling in the present, one forms what is grasped through the characteristic of karmic fruition;
by taking up craving and clinging in the present, one forms what is grasped through the characteristic of affliction;
and by taking up becoming in the present, one forms what is grasped through the characteristic of karma.
By taking up birth, old age, death, future consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact,
and feeling as the "appropriated," these twenty-four factors, through the accomplishment of that appropriation, become twenty.
As stated in the Abhidharma:

regarding the existence of the first karma, delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*), accumulation is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), attachment is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), seeking is grasping (*upādāna*), and intention is becoming (*bhava*). These five factors constitute the existence of this birth; the karma performed at the outset is its condition.

Not understanding consciousness and entering into delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*); their accumulation is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); attachment is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); seeking is grasping (*upādāna*); and intention is becoming (*bhava*). These five factors, within this karmic existence, serve as conditions for future birth and for the transition of consciousness at the time of future birth; this is called the purification of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-viśuddhi*).

This entry into what is touched is contact (*sparśa*), and this grasping is feeling (*vedanā*); these two dharmas exist in future birth (*upapatti-bhava*), and the karma performed therein is their condition (*pratyaya*).
Thus it should be understood through twenty aspects.
What is meant by "by way of the wheel"?

Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness, and so on, up to: conditioned by birth are aging and death. In this manner, the entire mass of suffering arises.
Ignorance regarding this entire mass of suffering is what is called "ignorance."
Regarding "ignorance conditions volitional formations," this should further be understood by means of the wheel.
How is it "drawn"? There are two ways of being drawn: namely, that which is initiated by ignorance and that which is initiated by old age and death.
Question:
What is the beginning of ignorance? Answer:
This explains the sequence.
What is the beginning of old age and death?
This is the sequence of transcendence.
Furthermore, that which begins with ignorance is the aspect of the limit of existence, known as the future.
That which begins with old age and death is the aspect of the initial limit, known as the past.
Thus it may be understood through association.
Question:
How is it understood through differentiation?
Answer: There are two kinds of causal conditions: mundane causal conditions and supramundane causal conditions.
Among these, that which begins with ignorance constitutes the mundane causal condition.
Question:
What are the causes and conditions for transcending the world? Answer:

Suffering depends on suffering; faith depends on faith; joy depends on joy; rapture depends on rapture; serenity depends on serenity; happiness depends on happiness; concentration depends on concentration; knowledge and vision according to reality depends on knowledge and vision according to reality; disenchantment depends on disenchantment; dispassion depends on dispassion; liberation depends on liberation; and the knowledge of cessation depends on the knowledge of cessation—this is called the supramundane causal condition.
Furthermore, four kinds of causes and conditions are taught:
karma and afflictions as causes, seeds as causes, and active and collective karma as causes.
Question:
What is meant by karma and afflictions being the cause?
Answer: They are initiated by ignorance.
What is meant by "having the seed as cause"?
It is like the continuity of the seed and the sprout.
What is meant by "having activity"?
Just like transformed matter (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*).
How is it that common karma serves as its cause?
It is like the earth, the snowy mountains, the oceans, the sun, and the moon.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
these material and mental phenomena do not have common karma as their cause; rather, time is their cause, and there is no such thing as common karma.
As the Blessed One said in a verse:
Karma is not shared with others; it is a treasure that cannot be stolen by another.
Whatever merit a person performs, they alone shall receive its wholesome retribution.
Thus may it be understood through discernment.
Question:
How are they subsumed by way of their characteristics? Answer:

There are four ways of inclusion: inclusion by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), inclusion by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*), inclusion by way of the elements (*dhātu*), and inclusion by way of the truths (*satya*).

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), contact (*sparśa*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Consciousness is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness.
Name-and-form is subsumed under four aggregates.
The six sense bases are subsumed under two aggregates.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Birth, aging, and death are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The factors of ignorance, formations, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-and-death are subsumed under the bases (*āyatana*).
Consciousness (vijñāna) is subsumed under the mental faculty (manāyatana).
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is subsumed under the five internal sense bases (pañcādhyātmikāyatanāni).
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are subsumed under the six internal sense bases.
Ignorance, volitional formations, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death are subsumed within the dharma-element.
Consciousness and the mind are subsumed within the consciousness-element.
Name-and-form is subsumed under five elements.
The six sense bases are subsumed under twelve truths.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping are subsumed under ten truths.
The remaining nine are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering.
The factors of the path, which are the supramundane causes and conditions, are subsumed under the Truth of the Path.
The cessation of those causes and conditions is subsumed under the Truth of Cessation.
Thus it should be understood through the inclusion of characteristics;
thus it should be understood through the skillful means of the causal conditions of practice.
This concludes the section on the skillful means of causal conditions.
*Vimuttimagga* (Treatise on the Path to Liberation), Scroll Ten; *Vimuttimagga*, Scroll Eleven.
Composed by the Arhat Upatissa, translated into the Liang language as "Great Radiance."
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Five Expedient Means, Part Two. Question:
What are the expedient means regarding the Noble Truths?

Answer: They are the Four Noble Truths: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Question:
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Answer:

The suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, the suffering of lamentation, the suffering of affliction, the suffering of suffering itself, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and, in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
The suffering of birth arises from the aggregates (*skandha*) within the various classes of sentient beings; this is the meaning of the accumulation of all suffering.

The suffering of old age consists in the maturation of the various elements (*dhātu*); it is the meaning of the loss of strength, physical form, the sense faculties (*indriya*), mindfulness, and wisdom.
The suffering of death means the extinction of the life-span; it carries the sense of being terrified.
The suffering of sorrow means that when one reaches a state of extreme pain, the mind becomes fearful; this carries the sense of internal burning.
The suffering of grief and lamentation means that when pain reaches the point of speech; this carries the sense of both internal and external burning.
The suffering of suffering refers to physical suffering; this is the meaning of the body being the cause of suffering.
The suffering of affliction refers to mental suffering; this is the meaning of the mind being the cause of suffering.
The suffering of association with the disliked refers to being joined with unlovely sentient beings; this is the meaning of creating suffering.
The suffering of separation from the beloved refers to being separated and parted from dear sentient beings; its meaning is the production of sorrow and pain.
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks refers to desiring to be separated from the unloved and desiring union with the loved, yet failing to obtain them; its meaning is the loss of happiness.

Regarding the brief explanation of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*): one does not escape the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging; therefore, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is explained briefly.
Question:
What are the five aggregates of clinging?
Answer: The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
This should be understood as it is explained at length in the *Kauśalya-vastu* (The Treatise on Skillfulness) regarding the aggregates.
Thus, there are two kinds of suffering: situational suffering (*sthāna-duḥkha*) and intrinsic suffering (*svabhāva-duḥkha*).

In this regard, birth-suffering, death-suffering, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and, in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—these are called situational suffering.
Suffering due to anxiety, suffering due to grief and lamentation, and suffering due to vexation—these are called suffering by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-duḥkha*).

As for the three types of suffering, they are: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
In this regard, bodily suffering and mental suffering are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
When tainted pleasant feelings (*sāsrava-sukha-vedanā*) perish in that state, it is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) are the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Question:
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? Answer:

Craving causes rebirth and arises together with desire; it arises everywhere as such craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
Regarding the statement "this craving causes rebirth": craving for existence predominantly brings about the arising of craving for birth.
Regarding the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*), it is craving alone that is its unique cause; therefore, it is called the origin of suffering.
That which arises together with desire is designated as "origin" because craving causes delight, and as "defilement" because it causes corruption.
Together with defilement, joy arises; that which arises is the locus, and the locus causes the nature of the body to arise—this is the locus of rapture.
This is the locus of lovely forms; this is the locus of rapture.

Thus, there are craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*). Excluding craving for existence and craving for non-existence, all other cravings are craving for sensual pleasure.
Craving for existence arises together with the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
That which is not craving for existence arises together with the view of annihilationism.
This is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.
Question:
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? Answer:
It is the remainderless fading away, relinquishing, detachment, liberation, and non-occurrence of craving alone; this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
Question:
This is not so. Since this too is both accumulation and cessation, why did the Blessed One speak of the cessation of the cause of suffering?

Answer: Because the cause of suffering is extinguished, it becomes non-arising and non-ceasing; this is the meaning that should be realized. Therefore, when accumulation is extinguished, the Blessed One speaks of the extinction of suffering.
Question:
What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? Answer:
It is this eightfold noble path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Right view is the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.
Right intention is the three types of wholesome intention.
Right speech is the abstention from the four unwholesome verbal actions.
Right action is the abstention from the three types of unwholesome conduct.
Right livelihood is the abstention from wrong livelihood.
Right effort consists of the four right strivings.
Right mindfulness refers to the four foundations of mindfulness. Right concentration refers to the four dhyānas.

Furthermore, if one practices the Noble Path, knowing and seeing Nirvāṇa is called right view; being fully aware of Nirvāṇa alone is right thought; abandoning wrong speech is right speech; abandoning wrong action is right action; abandoning wrong livelihood is right livelihood; abandoning wrong effort is right effort; mindfulness of Nirvāṇa is right mindfulness; and single-minded focus on Nirvāṇa is right concentration.

Thus, the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the basis of psychic power consisting of wisdom (*prajñā-ṛddhipāda*), and the factor of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) constitute the entry into internal right view.

The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), the basis of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*), the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*), the factor of awakening that is energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*) constitute the entry into internal energy.
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and the four foundations of mindfulness constitute entry into internal right mindfulness.

The faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the basis of psychic power of mind, the faculty of faith, the power of faith, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity constitute entry into internal right concentration.
These thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are comprised within the Eightfold Noble Path; this is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
These are the Four Noble Truths.
Question:
For what reason are the Four Noble Truths taught, rather than three or five? Answer:
All doubts are established as fourfold because they concern the causes and fruits of both the mundane and the supramundane.
Question:
How so? Suffering is the fruit of conventional truth; its cause is the accumulation of conventional truth. Cessation is the fruit of supramundane truth;
the Path is the cause of supramundane truth.
Therefore, there are four, neither three nor five.
Furthermore, one should know that because there are four categories—those to be known, those to be abandoned, those to be realized, and those to be cultivated—they constitute four.
These Four Noble Truths can be understood through eleven modes:

by way of the meaning of the phrases, by way of their characteristics, by way of their sequence, by way of their summary, by way of analogies, by way of analysis, by way of enumeration, by way of unity, by way of diversity, and by way of sequential inclusion. Thus they are extensively subsumed through these characteristics.
Question:
What is meant by "by way of the meaning of the phrases"? Answer:

Regarding the "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*): they are called "Noble Truths" because they were spoken by the Noble Ones (*ārya*), and because one becomes a Noble One through the thorough penetration of them.
"Truth" (*satya*) means that which is thus, that which is not otherwise, and that whose own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not otherwise.

"Suffering" has the meaning of result; "origination" has the meaning of cause; "cessation" has the meaning of following-extinction; and the "path" has the meaning of seeing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus, they may be understood through the meaning of these terms.
Question:
How is it by way of characteristics? Answer:

Suffering has the characteristic of affliction; its origin has the characteristic of causality; its cessation has the characteristic of non-arising; and the path has the characteristic of skillful means.

Furthermore, suffering has the characteristics of oppression, distress, conditioned existence, and finitude. Its origin has the characteristics of accumulation, causal condition, conjunction, and attachment. Its cessation has the characteristics of renunciation, tranquility, unconditioned existence, and the essence of clarified butter (*amṛta*). The path has the characteristics of a vehicle, that which brings one there, vision, and reliance.
Thus, their distinct characteristics can be known.
Question:
How are they to be understood according to their sequence?
Answer: The Truth of Suffering is taught first because it is coarse in meaning and because its realization is primary;
this suffering arises from the second [truth], Accumulation.
"This is the cessation of this accumulation; this is the cessation of this suffering"—this is the third [noble truth], Cessation.
"This is the means for true cessation"—this is the fourth [noble truth], the Path.
It is like a skilled physician who first identifies the source of a disease, then inquires about its causes, and finally prescribes medicine according to the illness in order to eliminate it.
Thus, this illness is to be understood as suffering;
thus, the causes and conditions of this illness are to be understood as its origination;
thus, the cessation of this illness is to be understood as liberation and extinction.
This medicine is to be understood as being like the Path.
It is to be understood in this way according to the sequence.
Question:
What is meant by "in brief"?
Answer: Birth is suffering; that which causes birth is the origin; the cessation of suffering is extinction; and that which leads to cessation is the path.
The locus of afflictions is suffering; afflictions are the origin. The cessation of afflictions is cessation; the means of their cessation is the path.

Suffering can give rise to and open the door of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the origin can give rise to and open the door of the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); cessation can give rise to and open the door of the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*); and the path can give rise to and open the door of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Thus it may be understood in brief.
Question:
How is this illustrated by analogy?
Answer: As with a poisonous tree, so may suffering be known.
As with a seed, so may its origin be known.
In this way, the burning of the seeds and their extinction can be known;
as with fire, so too can the Path be known.
Just as there is suffering and fear on this shore, so too can suffering be known.
As with the current, so should origination be understood.
As the far shore is without suffering and without fear, so should cessation be understood.
As a boat is able to cross over, so should the path be understood.
As the carrying of a burden, so should suffering be understood.
As the taking up of a burden, so should its origin be understood.
As the laying down of a burden, so should its cessation be understood.
Just as with the method of setting down a burden, so may the Path be understood.
Thus it may be known through analogy.
Question:
How can it be known through analysis? Answer:
There are four kinds of truths: the truth of speech, the individual truth, the ultimate truth, and the noble truth.
Thus, to speak what is true and not what is untrue is called the truth of speech (*vācasatya*).
To enter deeply into each respective truth through various views is called the respective truths (*pratyekasatya*).
For that monk, the quality of falsehood and delusion is not his truth; rather, the quality of non-falsehood and non-delusion is his truth.
Nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
It is that which is practiced by the noble ones; it is the noble truth.
It is the noble truth in which they find delight.
Thus it may be known through discrimination.
Question:
How may it be known through enumeration?
Answer: With the exception of craving, the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena of the three realms constitute the Truth of Suffering;
craving constitutes the Truth of Origination.
The abandonment of those [defilements] is the Truth of Cessation;
the Eightfold Path is the Truth of the Path.
Furthermore, with the exception of craving, the remaining afflictions, as well as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, constitute the Truth of Suffering in the Third Dhyāna.
Craving and the remaining afflictions are the truth of origination;
their abandonment is the truth of cessation;
and the path is the truth of the way.
Furthermore, with the exception of craving, all other afflictions and all unwholesome factors among the wholesome and indeterminate dharmas of the three realms constitute the Truth of Suffering;
craving and the afflictions, along with all unwholesome factors, constitute the Truth of Origination;
the abandonment of these constitutes the Truth of Cessation.
The Path is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Furthermore, with the exception of craving, afflictions, and all that is unwholesome, the unwholesome factors of the three stages and the indeterminate factors of the three stages constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*);
craving, the remaining afflictions, and all that is unwholesome, as well as the wholesome factors of the three stages, constitute this Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
The abandonment of that is the Truth of Cessation;
the Path is the Truth of the Path.
In this context, "craving" (tṛṣṇā) has the sense of seeking a flavor; "origination" (samudaya) has the sense of the fetters that bind existence; and the remaining afflictions are origination.
That which has the sense of being subject to abandonment and that which has the sense of causing existence to arise—these constitute all unwholesome states as "origination.
That which has the sense of causing existence to continue constitutes the wholesome dharmas of the three stages as "origination."

Thus, craving and the remaining afflictions constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). All unwholesome states in the three realms, as well as wholesome states, constitute either the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) or the Truth of Origination; because they are characterized by oppression, sorrow, and the conditioned nature of existence, they constitute the Truth of Suffering.
Because of the causal conditions for aggregation and attachment to the characteristic of conjunction, the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) is established.
This can be understood through enumeration.
Question:
How can they be known as one? Answer:

These Four Truths constitute a unity through four aspects: by way of the meaning of truth (*satya*), by way of the meaning of suchness (*tathatā*), by way of the meaning of dharma (*dharma*), and by way of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus it can be known by means of the one.
Question:
How can it be known by means of the manifold?
Answer: There are two truths: the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the supramundane truth (*lokottara-satya*).

As for the worldly truth, it consists of that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), with fetters (*saṃyojana*), with bonds (*bandhana*), with floods (*ogha*), with calamities (*vyasana*), with hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), tangible, involving grasping (*upādāna*), and characterized by affliction (*kleśa*); namely, suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

The supramundane truth is that which is untainted, without fetters, without bonds, without outflows, without calamities, without hindrances, intangible, without grasping, and without afflictions; it is what is called cessation and the path.
The three truths are conditioned; the truth of cessation is unconditioned. Three truths are formless; the truth of suffering is both with form and formless.
The truth of origination is unwholesome; the truth of the path is wholesome; the truth of cessation is indeterminate; the truth of suffering is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
The truth of suffering is to be known; the truth of origination is to be abandoned; the truth of cessation is to be realized; the truth of the path is to be cultivated.
Thus, it is to be understood in various ways.
Question:
How is it expanded by way of sequence? Answer:

By means of one kind [of contemplation]: the conscious body is suffering; the accumulation of the conceit "I am" is the origin; the abandonment of that is cessation; and mindfulness of the body is the path.
By way of two aspects: name-and-form are suffering and ignorance; craving for existence is the origin; the abandonment of these is cessation; and śamatha and vipaśyanā are the path.

It is established by way of three aspects: namely, the suffering of suffering is the Truth of Suffering; the three unwholesome roots are the Truth of Origination; the abandonment of those is Cessation; and morality, concentration, and wisdom are the Path.
It is established by way of four aspects:
the nature of the four bodies is suffering; the four perversions are the origin; the cessation of the perversions is cessation; and the four foundations of mindfulness are the path.
It is established by way of five aspects:
the five destinies are suffering; the five hindrances are the origin; the abandonment of the hindrances is cessation; and the five faculties are the path.
It is also established by way of six aspects:

The six bases of contact are suffering; the six groups of craving are the origin; the abandonment of the groups of craving is cessation; and the six factors of renunciation are the path. It is established by way of sevenfold sets:

the seven stations of consciousness are suffering; the seven underlying tendencies are the origin; the abandonment of the seven underlying tendencies is cessation; and the seven factors of enlightenment are the path.
It is established by way of eight aspects:
the eight worldly dharmas are suffering; the eightfold wrong path is the origin; the abandonment of the eightfold wrong path is cessation; and the eightfold right path is the way.
It is established by way of nine aspects:

the nine abodes of sentient beings are suffering; the nine factors rooted in craving are the origin; the abandonment of those is cessation; and the nine factors of the root of right attention are the path.
It is established by means of ten aspects:

the practice of the ten directions is suffering (*duḥkha*); the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the origin (*samudaya*); the severing of the fetters is cessation (*nirodha*); and the ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are the path (*mārga*).
Thus, it may be understood in detail according to this sequence.
Question:
How is it included? Answer:
There are three types of inclusion: inclusion by aggregates (*skandha*), inclusion by bases (*āyatana*), and inclusion by elements (*dhātu*).

Among these, the Truth of Suffering is included within the five aggregates; the Truth of Origination and the Truth of the Path are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and the Truth of Cessation is not included within any aggregate.

The Truth of Suffering is subsumed within the twelve bases (āyatana); the other three Truths are subsumed within the base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana). The Truth of Suffering is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu); the other three Truths are subsumed within the element of mental phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Thus it should be understood through inclusion.
By means of this practice, one brings about knowledge regarding the noble truths; this is called the application of the noble truths. The application of the noble truths is hereby concluded.

Chapter Twelve: Analysis of the Truths (*Vibhaṅga-satya-varga*), Part One of the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra*. At that time, the practitioner of meditation has already clearly understood the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and the truths of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). He has already acquired the training in the precepts (*śīla*), the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because he is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) not yet liberated from the fear of the miserable realms (*apāya*), he has contemplated the terror of the miserable realms; he has contemplated the terror of beginningless birth and death (*saṃsāra*); he has contemplated the impossibility of finding even a single moment [of permanence]; he has contemplated the analogy of being pierced by three hundred spears; and he has contemplated the analogy of the burning head. Yet, he has not yet analyzed the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*). In order to analyze these Noble Truths, he should apply skillful means, cultivate aspiration, and exert courageous diligence; with a focused mind, he should maintain mindfulness of the object until it is fully perfected.
Question:
How should one act? Answer:

That practitioner of meditation should first hear the Four Noble Truths—whether in brief, in detail, or both in brief and in detail—and should receive and uphold them through hearing, through their meaning, and through recitation.

At that time, the practitioner of meditation enters into a state of profound stillness and sits; with an undistracted mind and a mind free from coming and going, he should cause the Four Noble Truths to arise.

First, the Truth of Suffering should be caused to arise. This may be done by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), or the elements (*dhātu*). One should cause it to arise through their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and their correlation with the aggregates, as explained at length in the *Skandhopāya*; thus it should be understood.

Regarding the "entrances" (āyatana), one should cause them to arise through their association with the entrances, as explained at length in the section on the skillful means of the entrances; thus should it be understood.

Regarding the "elements" (dhātu), one should cause them to arise through their association with the elements, as explained at length in the section on the skillful means of the elements; thus should it be understood.

That practitioner of meditation, having thus [analyzed] the aggregates, bases, and elements, perceives that there are only aggregates, bases, and elements—neither a sentient being nor a life-principle—and having brought this about, he has attained the perception of formations.
At that time, two things have already been briefly established as arising, namely name (nāma) and form (rūpa).

Among these, the aggregate of form consists of the ten bases (āyatana) and ten elements (dhātu); the four aggregates consist of the mind base (manāyatana) and seven elements. These are called the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
Whether it be name or form, there are other names and other forms.
These other names and other forms are empty of form; form is empty of name; name is not separate from form, and form is not separate from name.
Just as the sound of a drum arises solely in dependence upon name-and-form (nāmarūpa),
and arises in dependence upon form and name, like a blind man and a lame man traveling together.
Question:
What is the distinction between name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)? Answer:
Name is bodiless; form is embodied.
Name has cognition; form has no cognition.
Name changes rapidly; form changes slowly.
Name has no accumulation; form has accumulation.
Name consists of perception, volition, and consciousness; form does not possess these.
Form consists of walking, leaning, sitting, lying down, bending, and stretching;
name does not possess these. Name knows: "I walk," "I lean," "I sit," "I lie down," "I bend," and "I stretch"; form does not possess this.
Regarding form (*rūpa*), there is no such thing as eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting;
regarding name (*nāman*), there is no such thing as "I know," "I drink," "I eat," "I chew," or "I taste.
Regarding form, there is no such thing as clapping, playing, laughing, weeping, or various kinds of speech; regarding name, there is no such thing.
"Name" refers to that which knows, "I," "me," "my," laughs, plays, cries, and engages in various forms of speech; form does not possess these.
This is called the differentiation between name and form.
That practitioner of meditation thus regards name and form as being merely name and form, devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a life-principle.
Having caused [the mind] to arise and having attained the perception of activity, at that time all [mental formations] are abbreviated.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, one causes the arising of pure knowledge and vision as it truly is, and causes name-and-form to arise.
This general discourse on the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) should be understood as having caused it to arise.
Once that practitioner of meditation has thus caused the Truth of Suffering to arise, they should form the conception of sentient beings and contemplate the causal conditions of this suffering.
Question:
What are the causes and conditions of this suffering, and how does it arise? Answer:

That practitioner of meditation understands thus: this suffering has birth as its causal condition; birth has becoming as its causal condition; becoming has grasping as its causal condition; grasping has craving as its causal condition; craving has feeling as its causal condition; feeling has contact as its causal condition; contact has the six sense bases as its causal condition; the six sense bases have name-and-form as their causal condition; name-and-form has consciousness as its causal condition; consciousness has volitional formations as its causal condition; and volitional formations have ignorance as their causal condition.

Thus, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness; and with birth as condition there is aging and death, giving rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. In this way, the entire aggregate of suffering comes into being.

In this way, that practitioner of meditation, having observed extensively how [the aggregates] are bound by causes and conditions, then performs a summary: "With feeling as condition, craving arises; that is the origination of suffering."

Whether it be the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), the noble knowledge of the causes and conditions (*ariya-paccayākāra-ñāṇa*), or the purification through the removal of doubt—these various expressions of speech give rise to knowledge regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudayasacca*).

When that practitioner of meditation has given rise to the knowledge of the origination of suffering and has transcended doubt within samādhi, he then contemplates the cessation of suffering. What is it that ceases?
It is for the cessation of suffering. What ceases?
It is this suffering that ceases.

That practitioner of meditation understands thus: from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of suffering; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of becoming; from the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of craving; and from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations.

In this way, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Thus, this entire mass of suffering comes to its cessation.

When that practitioner of meditation has thus extinguished the bonds of such conditions, having expanded and investigated them, he then performs a summary: "This feeling is conditioned by craving; from its cessation comes the cessation of suffering. Thus, he brings about the realization of the Truth of Cessation.
When that practitioner of meditation has thus caused the truth of cessation to arise, he then contemplates the path to the cessation of suffering:
"What is the path?
By what means is craving brought to cessation?"

That practitioner of meditation thus understands the five aggregates of clinging by contemplating their defects; this path and this equipment lead to the cessation of craving. One should understand that he gives rise to the Truth of the Path, as has been explained at length regarding the application of the truths.

That practitioner of meditation, having thus successively caused the Four Noble Truths to arise, then contemplates the five aggregates of clinging by means of the one hundred and eighty phenomena through successive synthesis and analysis. All form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; great or small; coarse or subtle; far or near—all such form he contemplates extensively as impermanent, extensively as suffering, and extensively as non-self.

In this way, regarding all sensation, all perception, all formations, and all consciousness—each aggregate (skandha) being analyzed through twelve dharma-gates—there are fifty-two for the five aggregates. These become sixty when the fifty-two are expanded; and by applying the view of impermanence, the view of suffering, and the view of non-self to each of these sixty, they become one hundred and eighty.

Furthermore, there are one hundred and eighty dharma-gates: the six internal bases, the six external bases, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, the six groups of volition, the six groups of craving, and the six types of applied thought and the six types of sustained thought.
These sixteen constitute sixty; these sixty consist of sixty views of impermanence, sixty views of suffering, and sixty views of non-self. These three sets of sixty constitute one hundred and eighty.

Throughout long periods of years, seasons, months, fortnights, days and nights, times, moments, and instants, conditioned phenomena proceed by revolving as the new replaces the old, just as a lamp flame proceeds by way of a continuous succession.

One contemplates conditioned formations as impermanent; one contemplates the suffering of the miserable realms, the fear of hunger and thirst, and the pursuit of what is sought, the separation from what is loved, and the afflictions of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
This continuity is associated with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

One contemplates and analyzes suffering within the formative forces, [seeing] how that which is produced arises from the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements; from causes and conditions; from the truths; and from the causal conditions of karma and its retribution. It is without a sentient being, immovable, without a substantial entity, and arises through the formation of the nature of the formative forces.

By means of the contemplation of non-self through analytical discernment, one contemplates the impermanence of conditioned form (rūpa) by way of the sense of cessation, the sense of dread as suffering, and the sense of non-self as unreality; in this manner, one performs a concise and extensive analysis of the impermanence and cessation of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).
"Suffering" has the sense of dread; "non-self" has the sense of unreality. Thus, one should perform this brief and extensive analysis.

Thereby, by means of the analysis of impermanence, one eliminates the perception of permanence; by means of the analysis of suffering, one eliminates the perception of pleasure; and by means of the analysis of non-self, one eliminates the perception of self.
Question:
How is impermanence extensively analyzed? Answer:

Seeing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are—neither having "conditioned" as their limit nor "cessation" as their limit—one gives rise to the mind toward the signless (*animitta*) and settles the mind in the signless realm; for this reason, impermanence is extensively analyzed.
Question:
How is it analyzed by way of suffering? Answer:

One causes the mind to feel dread toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); by generating the mind through the vow of volitional action (*abhisaṃskāra*), one brings peace to the mind within the state of non-volitional action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). For this reason, suffering is extensively analyzed.
Question:
How is selflessness extensively analyzed? Answer:
Seeing that all phenomena arise from others and from this grasping, one settles the mind in the realm of emptiness; therefore, non-self is extensively analyzed.

Thus, having analyzed the three realms of existence, the five destinies, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of sentient beings, one eliminates fear; this concludes the analysis through the wisdom that perceives them as lacking intrinsic reality.

That practitioner of meditation, having already analyzed the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) according to the three characteristics, causes himself to delight in entering [the path] with the desire to sever all conditioned formations (saṃskāra).

At that time, regarding the present internal five aggregates of clinging, he grasps their characteristics and brings about a thorough penetration of their arising and ceasing. In this way, he thoroughly penetrates this phenomenon: that what was unarisen appears as arisen, and that which has arisen ceases.
In this regard, there are three kinds of grasping at signs:
grasping at the sign of affliction (*kleśa*), grasping at the sign of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and grasping at the sign of insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Herein, when foolish worldlings encounter objects of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they give rise to the inverted perception of pleasure and permanence; with their initial mind, they skillfully grasp at signs and thereby become attached to afflictions, like a moth throwing itself into a lamp. This is called grasping at the sign of affliction.
Question:
How does one grasp the characteristics of meditative concentration? Answer:

In this regard, the practitioner of meditation, desiring to attain concentration, takes up the signs of each of the thirty-eight mental applications from the initial stage through right mindfulness and clear comprehension; he binds the mind to each individual application so that it does not wander, just as one might bind an elephant—this is called "taking the sign of concentration."
Question:
How does one grasp the sign (*nimitta*) of vipaśyanā? Answer:

One should constantly observe people with the wisdom of the initial mind, discerning the individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. One should joyfully desire to abandon and cultivate those characteristics, as if grasping a poisonous snake; this is called taking up the characteristic of *vipaśyanā*.
In this regard, one may find delight in grasping the signs of *vipaśyanā*.
Question:
How does one grasp the signs of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
Answer:
The characteristics of that consciousness of form are either the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element; or they are the eye-base or the body-base.
In this way, one contemplates those feelings according to their characteristics: whether they are pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
In this way, one contemplates those perceptions according to their characteristics: whether they are perceptions of forms or perceptions of mental phenomena.
Thus one contemplates the characteristics of the formations of activity, whether they be contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, or attention.
Thus one contemplates the characteristics of that consciousness, whether it be visual consciousness or mental consciousness.
Thus one contemplates each respective object of meditation; thus one correctly grasps its characteristic and causes it to arise properly.
Having caused it to arise in this way, one grasps the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Furthermore, one grasps the characteristics of the mind by means of two modes: by way of the object (*vastu*) and by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Question:
How does one grasp the characteristics of the mind by way of the object?
Answer:

Because this mind of mine arises with respect to these things, one should observe that it arises because of these matters of form, these matters of feeling, these matters of perception, these matters of mental formations, and these matters of consciousness; thus does my mind arise.
Thus one should observe: in that way, he grasps the characteristics of the mind through its objects.
Question:
How does he grasp the characteristics of the mind through mental attention (*manasikāra*)?
Answer: One should observe in this way: "As I attend to form, this mind arises;
as I attend to feeling, perception, and formations, my mind arises."
In this way one should observe; in this way one has already applied attention and grasped the characteristics of the mind.
Question:
How are those characteristics correctly grasped?
Answer: By means of this practice and these characteristics, one forms the perception of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to establish contemplation.
If one is further able to contemplate those characteristics by means of this practice and these characteristics, this is called the successful apprehension of those characteristics.
Regarding the thorough penetration of arising and ceasing: there is arising, there is ceasing, and there is the thorough penetration of both arising and ceasing.
In this regard, when form has already arisen and is present, its characteristic of arising is its emergence and its characteristic of change is its cessation.
Those two phrases are seen with the eye of wisdom.

One penetrates the arising and ceasing [of phenomena]: having experienced past feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness, they arise with the characteristic of birth and cease with the characteristic of change.
Those two phrases refer to seeing and penetrating the arising and ceasing with the eye of wisdom.

Furthermore, one penetrates the characteristic of arising through three modes, and penetrates the characteristic of cessation through three modes; that is, by way of cause, by way of condition, and by way of intrinsic nature.
Question:
How does one penetrate the characteristic of arising by means of the cause? Answer:
Craving, ignorance, and karma arise from the aggregates; these are seen with the eye of wisdom, and their arising-characteristic is penetrated through their causes.
How is the arising-characteristic penetrated through their conditions?

With food as condition, the aggregate of form arises; with contact as condition, the [other] three aggregates arise; with name-and-form as condition, the aggregate of consciousness arises. One sees this with the eye of wisdom, and through conditions, one penetrates the nature of arising.
Question:
How does one penetrate the characteristics of arising by means of its own flavor? Answer:

Just as the continuity of a lamp’s flame is uninterrupted, with each preceding and succeeding moment arising anew, one perceives this through its characteristics and with the eye of wisdom; through the penetration of its own flavor, the characteristic of arising is realized.
Thus, by means of causes and by means of the view of arising, one forms a view through the characteristic of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), thereby causing awakening to arise.

By means of conditions and by means of intrinsic flavor, one forms a view regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), forming a perception through its characteristics, so that awakening may be attained through the momentary ungraspability [of phenomena].
Thus, one penetrates the characteristic of arising through these three modes of practice.
Question:
How does one penetrate the characteristic of cessation through these three modes of practice?

Answer: Through the cessation of causes, the cessation of conditions, and the cessation of their own inherent nature, there is thus the cessation of craving, the cessation of ignorance, and the cessation of karma; the aggregates (skandhas) thereby reach cessation. Seeing this with the eye of wisdom, one penetrates the characteristic of cessation through the cessation of causes.
With the cessation of nutriment, the aggregate of form ceases;
with the cessation of contact, the [other] three aggregates cease;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the aggregate of consciousness ceases. Seeing this with the eye of wisdom, one penetrates the characteristic of cessation through the cessation of conditions.

Just as the continuity of a lamp’s flame is uninterrupted, one perceives with the eye of wisdom that what first existed undergoes cessation; through the penetration of its own nature, one realizes the characteristic of cessation.

Thus, by seeing the cessation of causes, one sees the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); by means of characteristics, one establishes what is seen; by means of the characteristic of non-arising, one awakens; by means of the cessation of conditions and by means of its own nature, one sees cessation.
The first vision is established through the characteristic of the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), which is realized through the awakening to the unobtainability of moments.
Question:
If one perceives the Truth of Suffering by means of its arising and ceasing, and perceives it through its characteristics, why should higher wisdom arise?
Answer: What is the use of giving rise to views regarding cessation?

By means of the characteristic of the Truth of Suffering, one attains the vision of what was previously unseen; that suffering becomes fulfilled, and one proceeds until the faults of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been seen as they truly are. Having already given rise to the mind from the characteristics of formations, the mind achieves transcendence regarding non-formations, having already seen the perils of all formations as they truly are.

Having already aroused the mind from the aspect of formations (*saṃskāra*), one attains mastery over what is not a formation; herein, the vision of suffering is brought to fulfillment because one has reached the limit.

It is just as when a bird surrounded by fire cannot yet escape its fear; if it has not yet reached the void, it perceives the fault of being encircled by fire and achieves flight into the void. At that time, its perception of the fear of being encircled by fire is fulfilled in this manner—this should be understood here.
Thus, by means of causes, by means of conditions, and by means of the vision of arising, one achieves penetration into the characteristics of dependent origination:
"When this exists, that arises; because this arises, that comes to be."
Due to the cessation of causes and the cessation of conditions, by seeing the cessation of causes and conditions, one achieves thorough penetration of the characteristic of arising.
This being absent, this does not come to be; this ceasing, this ceases.
By means of its own flavor and by means of its arising and ceasing, having seen what has already arisen, one achieves penetration.

One knows that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); one knows their arising, one knows their cessation, and one also knows their duration.

In this way, by means of the vision of arising and ceasing, one understands that the four dharmas constitute the objects of knowledge: namely, the dharma of a single characteristic, the dharma of manifold characteristics, the dharma of non-substantiality, and the true dharma. Thus, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) that arise through attachment to a single continuity are seen not to constitute manifold grasping; nor do the formations that evolve from beginning to end constitute such grasping. Through the vision of cessation, they are seen not to constitute a single grasping; they are formations whose intrinsic nature is detached and immovable.

Because the views of beginning and end do not establish the grasping at a self, and because the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that evolve through causes and conditions are likewise seen as such, the view of phenomena does not establish the grasping at a non-existent entity.

Unlearned worldlings, through one kind of non-awakening, speak of permanence and annihilation; through various kinds of non-awakening, they speak of permanence; and through non-awakening regarding the non-existence of an entity, they speak of a self.
Thus, by means of the Dharma, non-awakening is established as the discourse on "non-activity.

Therein, through the language of equality and the language of the excellence of the single characteristic, various characteristics are subsumed to form a single characteristic; through the meaning of differentiation, the manifold is established;
through the meaning of affliction, a single nature is established; and through the meaning of skillful means, manifold natures are established.
Through the fruit of craving, one nature is established; through the fruit of karma, various natures are established.
That practitioner of meditation thus perceives this single nature and does not, in this regard, cling to the view of diversity;
if he perceives diverse natures, he does not, in this regard, cling to the view of permanence as a single nature.
If one perceives a single nature, then other actions and other cognitions remove this perception;
if one perceives a manifold nature, then those respective actions and cognitions remove this perception.
If one perceives a single nature, this removes the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
If one directly perceives various natures, this eliminates the view of permanence.
As that practitioner of meditation thus observes arising and ceasing, seeing both the single nature and various natures, how does the illumination of the Dharma arise?
When various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) manifest, one sees that they are without substantial reality (*avastuka*). Why?

Because all conditioned phenomena are without substance and are immovable; they have no further arising or abiding, but abide in their own nature (*svabhāva*), with causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) gathering together as their causal basis.

In this way, one causes the dharma of *śamatha* to arise by means of its arising; therein, through the sense of being without life-force and the sense of immovability, the dharma of non-substantiality (*avastuka*) can be known.
Through the sense of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the sense of conditions (*pratyaya*), the dharma of *śamatha* can likewise be known.
To cause the cessation-dharma (śamatha) to appear as non-substantial is called the "dharma," and to cause that same cessation-dharma to appear as the activity of karma is called "practice" (caryā).

Thus, by means of the dharma of single nature, one realizes the characteristic of suffering and achieves thorough penetration; by means of the dharma of manifold natures, one realizes the characteristic of impermanence and achieves thorough penetration.
By means of the dharma of non-substantiality, one realizes in this way the characteristic of selflessness through the dharma of tranquility and achieves thorough penetration.
Question:

Does that practitioner of meditation observe the arising and passing away of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) by means of the "without remainder" method, or should they observe them by means of the "one-pointed" method? Answer:

In the initial stage of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one grasps their characteristics; by penetrating their arising and ceasing without remainder, one brings all conditioned phenomena to fulfillment.
It is like a person who, tasting water at a single spot in the great ocean with their tongue, immediately knows that all its water is salty.
Thus it should be understood here:

one fulfills all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through two modes—by means of the objective basis and by means of non-delusion—and therein grasps their common characteristics, penetrating their arising and ceasing.
Those formations are fulfilled through the accomplishment of their respective functions; therein, because ignorance is severed, the remaining formations are fulfilled through non-delusion.

Therein lies the knowledge of arising and ceasing, which is the analytical knowledge of all formations: all formations are analyzed by way of the beginning limit of their arising, and analyzed by way of the subsequent limit of their cessation;
they are analyzed by way of the beginning limit of their arising becoming tranquil, and analyzed by way of the limit of existence being extinguished in its cessation.
Since arising follows from arising, there is no beginning; since ceasing follows from ceasing, there is no end.
Therefore, through the knowledge of arising and ceasing, one accomplishes the analytical knowledge of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). This concludes the knowledge of arising and ceasing.

That practitioner of meditation, thus perceiving the characteristics of arising and ceasing and skillfully discerning all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), delights in attaining the bliss of cessation and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
At that time, they do not direct their attention to observing arising, but perceive only the cessation of the mind.
By means of the matter of form, by means of the arising and ceasing of the mind, one observes the cessation of the mind based on that matter.

Likewise, by means of the matter of feeling, the matter of perception, the matter of formations, and the matter of consciousness, one observes the arising and ceasing of the mind based on those matters.
Furthermore, cessation is seen in this way through three modes: by way of grouping, by way of pairs, and by way of analysis.
Question:
How is it by way of grouping?
Answer: Regarding the postures and the mental states and mental factors arising from those postures, one perceives their cessation there by means of the perception of the aggregate.

Furthermore, having observed that form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, and consciousness is impermanent, at that time, one perceives the cessation of the mental states and mental factors arising from those impermanent phenomena by means of the perception of the aggregate.
In this way, one should view the aggregates through the lens of suffering and non-self.
Question:
How [should they be viewed] by way of pairs?
Answer: Having contemplated that this form is impermanent, one contemplates its impermanence; following that impermanence, the mind arises and one perceives the arising and ceasing of the mind.

Likewise, having contemplated that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one contemplates their impermanence; following those impermanent phenomena, the mind arises and one perceives their arising and ceasing.
Thus, having already established the fact of suffering and the fact of non-self, one should contemplate them as a pair in this manner.
Question:
How are they to be distinguished?
Answer:

Having already contemplated this form as impermanent, one gives rise to a mind that accords with the phenomenon of impermanence and perceives the arising and ceasing of the mind; thus, through analytical contemplation, one perceives the cessation of many minds.

Thus one contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; following the phenomenon of impermanence, one gives rise to the mind and observes the arising and ceasing of the mind. By means of this observation of the mind’s cessation, one further observes its extinction; in this way, through analytical observation, one perceives the extinction of many minds.
Thus one contemplates suffering and contemplates non-self; having thus made this distinction, one realizes only the cessation of that [suffering].
When the task of the cessation of suffering is accomplished with single-mindedness, one constantly seeks the moments of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and attains benefit.
That practitioner of meditation, by means of this wisdom and not through any other condition, perceives the entire world.

Just as one sees the nature of things as being like the tip of a mustard seed, undergoing the changes of birth, aging, and death within a single moment of consciousness, at that time the practitioner of meditation perceives it in such a manner once again.
As stated in the verse:
This pair, the nature of name-and-form, Mutually perishes as one ceases;
When the phrase ceases, that [other] ceases, Along with what is produced by its causes.
The aggregates are impermanent and subject to cessation; they are phenomena that arise in suffering and then cease.
Just as the sound produced by striking a drum with a mallet does not arise from the eye, so too the five factors—form, fragrance, and the rest—do not arise from form.
Nor does it exist apart from these two phrases; conditioned phenomena arise in dependence on conditions.
Just as the sound produced by striking a drum with a mallet does not arise from the ear, so too the five factors such as form and fragrance do not arise from the sound.
Nor is it apart from these two phrases.
The five dharmas, such as form and fragrance, do not arise from fragrance,
nor are they apart from these two phrases.
The five dharmas, such as color and fragrance, do not arise from taste,
nor are they apart from these two categories.
The five dharmas, such as color and fragrance, do not arise from touch either.
Nor is it apart from these two phrases.
It does not arise from the form of the sense-base, nor does it emerge from the sphere of phenomena; it arises dependent upon causes and conditions.
Just as the sound of a drum is produced by the striking of a mallet, so too do those faculties emerge when they are most feeble.
The initial cause is also most feeble; that cause is also most feeble, and what arises from it is likewise feeble. Together with the ground, this is most feeble;
